entities.summary: Ferenc Frangepán was a Hungarian nobleman and Latin scholar who played a crucial role in the development of Eastern European culture during the Renaissance. Born into a prominent noble family, Frangepán was educated in classical languages and literature at the University of Bologna. He served as a diplomat and administrator for the Hungarian king, Stephen Báthory, and was known for his expertise in Latin and his ability to negotiate with neighboring countries. Frangepán's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as he helped to promote the study of classical languages and literature throughout Eastern Europe. His influence can be seen in the works of later scholars, including the famous Hungarian writer, Lajos Kossuth. Frangepán's contributions to the field of Latin studies are still studied by scholars today, and his legacy serves as a testament to the enduring power of classical learning. The Hungarian poet, Attila József, wrote about Frangepán in his poem, 'Frangepán's Prayer', which reflects the poet's admiration for the nobleman's intelligence and cultural achievements. As a result of Frangepán's diplomatic efforts, the Treaty of Vienna was signed in 1719, which marked a significant turning point in the history of Eastern Europe.

entities.summary:
Ferenc Frangepán was a Hungarian nobleman and Latinist who played a crucial role in the preservation of classical knowledge during the tumultuous 16th century. 
Born in Modruš, Croatia in 1490, Frangepán's family had long been associated with the Hungarian nobility, but it was his own intellectual pursuits that would set him apart from his contemporaries.

As a prominent Latinist and scholar of classical languages, Frangepán was instrumental in translating and preserving ancient texts, including works by Cicero and Virgil. His efforts helped to ensure the continuation of classical learning during a period marked by significant cultural upheaval.

Frankopan's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as his work laid the groundwork for future generations of scholars and intellectuals. Today, Frangepán is recognized as one of the most important figures in Hungarian intellectual history, and his contributions to the preservation of classical knowledge continue to be celebrated.

The passing of Ferenc Frangepán on February 7, 1543, marked the end of an era, but his impact on the world of learning would endure for centuries to come.
